attributes.title: Level 6

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create 2 arrays to store the Player and Enemy sprite image variables?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the images in the runningAnimation and batAnimation be used for? 

❓ Why might there be 3-4 similar images stored in each array?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The images in the 2 arrays will be used to animate the images of sprites in this project. Storing the images as variables and in an array helps make the animation code more organized and easier for the coder to read.
steps.instructions:
Create an array of animated image frames for the Player and Enemy sprites. 


Notice there are image variables under the comment // Player sprite image animation. Underneath, use the keyword let to declare a new array called runningAnimation. Type an assignment operator and a pair of brackets [ ] with the names of the 4 “running” image variables typed inside, separated by commas. 


Under the comment // Enemy sprite image animation, after the image variable code, follow the same steps to store the Enemy sprite images in a new array called batAnimation.


Now, the running Player sprite images and the Enemy sprite images are stored in 2 arrays to be used in the project.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you position the Enemy sprite in an appropriate location for the background selected?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What image might you use as the background in this project?

❓ Where might the Enemy sprite appear on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider where the Enemy sprite might appear on screen, given their background image. In the next step, the Enemy sprite’s image will be animated, which may inform what area of the screen the sprite should appear in.
steps.instructions:
Add a background image to the project and create an Enemy sprite!


Open Scene and drag [set background image to (img)] under // game set up. Select a “haunted castle” background from the gallery.


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] under setBackgroundImage. Update the sprite name to “bat”, then replace img`...` with one of the Enemy image variable names. Update the sprite kind to Enemy.


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] under sprites.create. Update the position of the Enemy sprite to place it near the castle on screen.


Click ▶ to see the background image and the Enemy sprite appear on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the sprite, frames, frameInterval, and loop parameters in the runImageAnimation function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens to the Enemy sprite when the animation code is run?

❓ How is the batAnimation array used to set the frames parameter in the runImageAnimation function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the project is run, the Enemy sprite’s image loops through the 3 images stored in the batAnimation array. The images loop through every 500 milliseconds and will continue to loop while the project is played.

💡 Explain to the ninja that several images img`` can also be added inside the brackets [] to set the frames parameter in the runImageAnimation function. However, using an array to store the image variables is cleaner and more organized, than using the array name in the frames parameter. In this case, the brackets are not needed and just the array name can be used as the argument.
steps.instructions:
Animate the Enemy sprite!


Click Animation, then drag [animate (mySprite) frames (frames) interval (ms) (500) loop (loop)] under the Enemy sprite code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

animation.runImageAnimation(mySprite, [], 500, false)


The runImageAnimation function takes 4 parameters: sprite, frames, frameInterval, and loop. Replace mySprite with the Enemy sprite name as the sprite parameter. Replace [] with the batAnimation array as the frames parameter. Leave the default 500 milliseconds as the frameInterval parameter. Replace false with true as the loop parameter.


Now, the Enemy sprite is animated with the images from the array of Enemy sprite images, and will loop through the different frames at the interval indicated in the frameInterval parameter.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprite animation on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the sprite, frames, frameInterval, and loop parameters in the runImageAnimation function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens to the Player sprite when the animation code is run?

❓ How is the runningAnimation array used to set the frames parameter in the runImageAnimation function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the project is run, the Player sprite’s image loops through the 4 images stored in the runningAnimation array. The images loop through every 500 milliseconds and continue to loop while the project is played.

💡 Explain to the ninja that several images img`` can also be added inside the brackets [] to set the frames parameter in the runImageAnimation function. However, using an array to store the image variables is cleaner and more organized, than using the array name in the frames parameter. In this case, the brackets are not needed and just the array name can be used as the argument.
steps.instructions:
Create a Player sprite and use animation to make it look like it’s running away from the castle!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] under the Enemy sprite code. Update the sprite name, then replace img`...` with one of the running sprite image variable names. 


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] under sprites.create. Update the position of the Player sprite to be at the entrance of the castle.


Click Animation, then drag [animate (mySprite) frames (frames) interval (ms) (500) loop (loop)] under the Player sprite code. 


Replace mySprite with the Player sprite name and [] with the runningAnimation array. Replace 500 milliseconds in the frameInterval parameter with a different interval value. Replace false with true to loop the animation image frames.


Set the depth level of the Player sprite by setting the Player sprite’s z-position to 4, so it appears in front of the other sprites.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite animation on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use a changeScale with a decimal value parameter inside an onUpdateInterval loop so that the Player sprite appears larger as it runs “closer”?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the onUpdateInterval loop runs?

❓ What argument might be used in the changeScale code so that the Player sprite increases by a small amount, each time the loop runs?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the onUpdateInterval loop runs, the Player sprite will grow a little larger from its center.

💡 Point out to the ninja that they should use a decimal value between 0 and 1 to set the value parameter in the changeScale code. Ask the ninja how much they’d like the Player sprite to grow each time and help them find a decimal value to reflect this, as needed.
steps.instructions:
Make the Player sprite appear larger as it runs “closer”!


Open Game and drag [run code on game update every (period) ms] under the existing Player sprite code. 


Open Sprites and drag [change (mySprite) scale by (1) anchor (ScaleAnchor.Middle)] inside the curly brackets of the onUpdateInterval loop. Replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name, then change the value parameter from 1 to a decimal value between 0 and 1, so that the sprite grows a little bit larger each time the loop runs. Use the default anchor property ScaleAnchor.Middle, so that the Player sprite grows from its center. 


Tinker with the period parameter of onUpdateInterval to change the rate the Player sprite grows!

 

Click ▶ to see the Player sprite grow larger as time passes!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select a new pathString parameter in the runImageAnimation function from the code completion tool?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What sprite might you add movement animation to?

❓ What movement type might you use to animate the sprite in the pathString parameter?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to look through the variety of pathString movement options in the code completion tool and consider which type of movement might fit the select sprite and background. 

💡 When the runImageAnimation function runs, the sprite selected will move in the path specified in the pathString parameter for 2000 milliseconds. The sprite’s movement will loop throughout the project.
steps.instructions:
Create another animated sprite in the project!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] under the Player sprite code. Update the sprite name, then select a sprite image from the gallery. 


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] under sprites.create. Update the position of the sprite.


Click Animation, then drag [animate (mySprite) with (pathString) for (ms) (2000) loop (loop)] under the sprite code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:


animation.runMovementAnimation(mySprite, animation.animationPresets

(animation.flyToCenter), 2000, false)


The runImageAnimation function takes 4 parameters: sprite, pathString, duration, and loop. Replace mySprite with the sprite name as the sprite parameter. In the pathString parameter, delete .flyToCenter, then type a dot operator and select a movement type from the code completion tool. Leave the default 2000 milliseconds as the duration parameter. Replace false with true as the loop parameter.


Click ▶ to see the sprite move in a loop.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you compose a short melody using stringPlayable function and update the tempo parameter?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is creating a custom melody in the JavaScript editor similar and different to creating custom melody in the blocks editor?

❓ What notes might be used in the custom melody to match the theme of the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that a melody is a short series of notes composed in a string and the tempo sets the rate to play the melody at in beats per minute. In the blocks editor, they were able to manually select a series of colored squares to create a custom melody. In the JavaScript editor, these notes can be represented by letters A-G and a number 1-8 indicating their octave. 

💡 Explain to the ninja that tempo is the speed at which a melody will play. A tempo of 60 will play at one beat per second, whereas the default tempo of 120 will play at two beats per second. Encourage the ninja to tinker with the parameter value to find the right speed for their melody.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out their melody and iterate on it to create a sound that matches the project. Remind them to use spaces between each note and to use a dash (-) to create rests, or pauses, between the notes of the melody.

💡 If the melody is not loud enough, encourage the Ninja to drag out the [set volume (20)] from Music to adjust the volume. They should replace 20 with a larger value, playtest the sound, then increase the volume as needed.
steps.instructions:
Add music to the project!


Open Music and drag [play (toPlay) (playbackMode)] underneath // music loop. Change melodyPlayable to stringPlayable.


The stringPlayable function takes 2 parameters: melody and tempo. Inside the parentheses, delete music.baDing then update the melody string to be a series of note names inside the quotation marks, represented by the letters A-G, with a number 1-8 following the letter to indicate the note’s octave. Use a dash - in the code to create a rest (a beat of silence). The code might look like: ﻿“C2 D2 F2 D2 C2 - B1”


Update the tempo, or the speed at which the melody is played, by changing the number of beats per minute.


Update music.PlaybackMode.UntilDone to make the melody play on repeat while the project is running by changing UntilDone to LoopingInBackground. 


Click ▶ to hear the music on loop in the project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses image and movement animation to code sprites to move in different ways on screen. Create a unique melody for the project, too!

validationItems.text: Create runningAnimation and batAnimation arrays to hold animation frames for the Player and Enemy sprites.
Add an Enemy sprite, set its position, and animate its appearance.
Add a Player sprite, set its position, animate its appearance, and set its depth.
Use an onUpdateInterval loop to change the player sprite’s scale over time.
Add a third sprite, set its position, and animate it with a preset.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 6 of Purple Belt! Before you create your final Purple Belt project, there are a few neat tricks to learn that could take your game to the next level! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 6:

badges.title: Extension Explorer
badges.description: Use animation and music code, plus the scroller and story extensions, to enhance a project.

badges.title: Stop Motion
badges.description: Use an array of images to create an animation for a sprite.

badges.title: Path of Least Resistance
badges.description: Use an animation preset path to animate a sprite’s movement.

badges.title: Earworm
badges.description: Create a custom melody using a string of note names.

badges.title: Seven Layer Dip
badges.description: Use the Scroller extension to change the background image layers.

badges.title: Parallax Party
badges.description: Use the Scroller extension to move a background layer to create a parallax effect.

badges.title: The Choice is Yours
badges.description: Use the Story extension to present the player with choices.

badges.title: Stage Directions
badges.description: Use the Story extension to move a sprite to a specific position.

badges.title: What’s my Line?
badges.description: Use the Story extension to have a sprite say text with custom colors.
